## Assessment: Ro60 (gene RO60) as an SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity (UniProt):** The record confirms RO60 / accession **P10155** is the "RNA-binding protein RO60," a 538-aa protein that binds Y RNAs and misfolded non-coding RNAs — i.e., the Ro protein of the **Ro/La ribonucleoprotein particle**. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P10155/entry

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold):** The predicted structure is high quality — mean pLDDT **93.3/100 (Very high)**. This supports a well-defined fold but is a structural-reliability metric, not disease evidence. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P10155

**Literature (Europe PMC):** Published work ties Ro/SSA autoantibodies to lupus and connective-tissue disease serology:
- "Mapping organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus" (2026) — SLE autoantigen-focused. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094
- "Autoantibodies as Precision Tools in Connective Tissue Diseases" (2026). https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41562780
- "The Art of Interpreting Antinuclear Antibodies (ANAs) in Everyday Practice" (2025). https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40806943

A note on honesty: my literature queries returned a mix of on-topic SLE papers and several Sjögren's/ILD-focused results (Ro antibodies span those conditions), so the search hits are partly tangential rather than a clean, SLE-only panel.

**Reasoning per criteria:** UniProt establishes that RO60 is the Ro protein — the recognized core component of the **Ro/La particle**, one of the named SLE autoantigen complexes, captured by the clinical **anti-Ro/La (anti-SSA)** antibody test. Under the stated rules, documented membership as a core component of a recognized SLE autoantigen complex is itself sufficient to classify it as an established autoantigen. The literature further corroborates its role in lupus/CTD autoantibody profiling.

**Caveat for your review:** The tools gave me strong identity/complex evidence (UniProt) plus supporting but somewhat mixed literature; none of the returned papers was a single definitive "anti-Ro60 in SLE" validation study, so you may want to confirm with a targeted clinical reference.

VERDICT: YES

Here is my assessment based on the tool evidence gathered.

## Assessment: Ro52 / TRIM21 as an SLE autoantigen

**Identity and complex membership (UniProt).** The protein is the "E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase TRIM21" (gene *TRIM21*, accession **P19474**, 475 aa). Critically, UniProt describes it as existing "as a ribonucleoprotein particle... composed of a single polypeptide and one of four small RNA molecules," explicitly notes "tissue specific differences in **RO/SSA proteins**," and states its common feature is the ability "to bind **HY RNAs**." This directly documents Ro52/TRIM21 as a recognized component of the **Ro/La (SSA/SSB) ribonucleoprotein particle** — the named SLE autoantigen complex captured by the clinical anti-Ro/SSA antibody test. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P19474/entry

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold).** The AlphaFold predicted structure has a mean pLDDT of **90.7/100 ("Very high")**, indicating a reliable predicted 3D model. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P19474

**Published literature (Europe PMC).** Multiple papers tie anti-Ro52/TRIM21 autoantibodies to lupus and the SLE autoantigen landscape:
- "Mapping organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus" (2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094
- "The pathogenic role of high-titer anti-Ro52 antibodies in neonatal lupus erythematosus" (2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42909017
- "High Immunological Activity and the Re-Evaluation of Anti-SSA/SSB Antibodies as Prognostic Markers for Major Organ Damage in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus" (2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42735434
- "Distinct IgM and IgG autoantibody profiles characterize incomplete and classified systemic autoimmune diseases" (2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42389530

**Interpretation and caveats.** The UniProt record establishes Ro52/TRIM21 as a core RO/SSA particle component, which under the stated criteria (recognized Ro/La autoantigen captured by the anti-Ro/SSA clinical test) is sufficient to classify it as an established SLE autoantigen. The literature reinforces this, with anti-Ro52 antibodies documented in neonatal lupus and SLE. One honest caveat for the expert reviewer: anti-Ro52/TRIM21 is notably *not specific* to SLE — the search also surfaced strong associations with interstitial lung disease, myositis, and Sjögren's syndrome. So while it is an established lupus autoantigen, it is a cross-disease autoantigen rather than an SLE-exclusive marker.

VERDICT: YES

## Assessment: La/SSB (gene SSB) as an SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity (UniProt).** The gene SSB encodes the protein whose official UniProt name is literally **"Lupus La protein"** (accession P05455, 408 aa). Its documented function is binding the 3′ poly(U) terminus of nascent RNA polymerase III transcripts, protecting and maturing them. The database name itself directly ties this protein to lupus. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P05455/entry

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold).** The predicted structure has a mean pLDDT of 74.5/100 ("Confident" band). This is a structural-reliability note only and does not bear on autoantigen status. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P05455

**Literature evidence (Europe PMC).** A search targeting "La SSB autoantigen SLE anti-La/SSB antibody" returned SLE autoantigen–focused work, including:
- "Mapping organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus" (2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094
- "The fluorescence patterns of antinuclear antibodies..." (2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42923724

A refined follow-up search ("anti-La/SSB antibodies Ro La ribonucleoprotein particle lupus clinical") returned further SLE-centered studies (e.g., protein biomarkers of inflammation in SLE — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42810773).

**Honest caveats for your review.**
- The strongest and most direct tool evidence is the UniProt record, which names the protein "Lupus La protein." The anti-La/SSB antibody is a recognized clinical test of the Ro/La ribonucleoprotein particle, consistent with my scope guidance treating Ro/La-particle components as established SLE autoantigens.
- However, the UniProt "subunit/complex" field I retrieved listed only interactions with DDX15/RUFY1 and did **not** explicitly document Ro60/La-particle core membership in the tool output.
- The literature hits are topically about SLE autoantigens broadly rather than crisp single-sentence confirmations specific to La/SSB; I did not retrieve a paper that states the anti-La/SSB–SLE association in isolation.

On balance, the tool evidence (UniProt naming the protein "Lupus La protein" plus SLE autoantigen-landscape literature surfaced by La/SSB-specific queries) supports recognition of La/SSB as an SLE autoantigen, with the caveat that my tools gave more direct evidence via the protein name than via an explicit complex-membership field or a single definitive paper.

VERDICT: YES

Here is my assessment based on the tool evidence.

## Assessment: Sm-B/B' (SNRPB, P14678) as an SLE autoantigen

**Identity and complex membership (UniProt P14678)**
SNRPB encodes the "Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein-associated proteins B and B'." UniProt establishes that it is one of the **seven common core Sm proteins** (SNRPB, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF, SNRPG) that assemble into the heptameric Sm ring forming the core of the spliceosomal U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNPs. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P14678/entry

This is directly relevant: the Sm core / snRNP is a recognized SLE autoantigen complex, captured by the clinical **anti-Sm** antibody test, and Sm-B/B' is a documented core component of that complex.

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold P14678)**
Mean pLDDT 69.5/100 — a "Low" confidence band. This reflects that much of the protein (notably its arginine-rich C-terminal tail) is likely disordered, and is a caveat about the *predicted 3D model*, not about its autoantigen status. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P14678

**Published literature (Europe PMC)**
- A 2001 study explicitly on "Lupus autoantibodies recognize the product of an alternative open reading frame of SmB/B'" — direct evidence that SLE patient autoantibodies target SmB/B'. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/11478783
- A 2024 study on "Smith-specific regulatory T cells" in lupus nephritis, reflecting the central role of the Smith (Sm) antigen system in SLE. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38321013

**Summary**
The evidence converges: UniProt documents SNRPB/Sm-B/B' as a recognized core component of the Sm/snRNP complex (the target of the clinical anti-Sm test), and the literature includes a lupus-specific study showing autoantibody recognition of SmB/B'. Per the stated criteria, core membership of the Sm complex plus documented clinical-antibody capture is sufficient to classify it as an established SLE autoantigen. The only caveat (low AlphaFold confidence) concerns the structural model, not autoantigenicity.

VERDICT: YES

## Assessment: Sm-D1 (SNRPD1) as an SLE autoantigen

**Identity and complex membership (UniProt P62314):** Sm-D1 is the "Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein Sm D1," a **core component of the Sm protein ring** shared by the spliceosomal U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNPs. UniProt explicitly lists it among the seven common Sm core proteins (SNRPB, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF, SNRPG) that assemble on snRNA to form the core snRNP. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P62314/entry

This is decisive for classification: the Sm core / snRNP is a recognized SLE autoantigen complex captured by the named clinical **anti-Sm** antibody test, and Sm-D1 is a documented core component of it.

**Published clinical evidence (Europe PMC):** The literature directly supports Sm-D1 as a clinically relevant SLE autoantigen:
- Anti-SmD1 antibodies associated with renal disorder, seizures, and pulmonary arterial hypertension in active SLE patients (Hu et al., 2017): https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28790444
- Evaluation of anti-SmD1 (aa 83–119) peptide reactivity in children with SLE (Yang et al., 2016): https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27900999
- SmD-derived peptides used in SLE diagnostic accuracy studies (Mahler et al., 2007): https://europepmc.org/article/MED/17640359
- SmD1 described as "the major SmD1 autoantigen" with lupus-derived autoantibodies binding its C-terminal peptide (Dieker et al., 2006): https://europepmc.org/article/MED/16540553

**Structural note (AlphaFold P62314):** The predicted structure is of "Confident" quality (mean pLDDT 82.8/100). This is a structural-confidence metric only and is not itself evidence of autoantigenicity. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P62314

**Summary for your review:** Both lines of tool evidence converge. UniProt documents Sm-D1 as a recognized core Sm/snRNP component (the anti-Sm target), and multiple clinical papers report anti-SmD1 autoantibodies in SLE patients with disease associations. The evidence is consistent, not conflicting. (As always, please verify the primary sources before use.)

VERDICT: YES

## Assessment: Sm-D2 (SNRPD2) as an SLE autoantigen

UniProt explicitly states it is one of the heptameric Sm core proteins (SNRPB, SNRPD1, **SNRPD2**, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF, SNRPG) that assemble on the snRNA to form the core snRNP of the U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNPs. (Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P62316/entry)

- **AlphaFold (P62316):** The predicted structure has a mean pLDDT of 90.6/100 — "Very high" confidence. (Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P62316) — This is a structural-reliability note, not autoantigen evidence.

- **Literature (Europe PMC):** My searches did not surface a focused, on-topic paper specifically about anti-Sm-D2 serology — returned results were largely peripheral or off-topic (e.g., general SLE autoantibody/complement studies, systemic sclerosis). So I have no direct paper-level citation to offer for Sm-D2 specifically.

**Interpretation (per the stated criteria):**

The Sm core (the common set of Sm proteins) is one of the recognized SLE autoantigen complexes, captured clinically by the **anti-Sm antibody test**. UniProt documents that Sm-D2 is an established *core component* of that Sm protein ring — not merely an interactor. Under the rule that complex-level evidence plus documented core membership is sufficient, Sm-D2 qualifies as an established SLE autoantigen on the basis of the UniProt membership evidence.

**Caveat for your review:** The judgment rests on tool-confirmed **complex membership** (UniProt), since my literature searches did not return a Sm-D2-specific paper. Note also that within the Sm complex, Sm-D1 and Sm-D3 are classically described as the most immunodominant anti-Sm targets; a protein-specific literature check for Sm-D2 reactivity would strengthen this. The evidence here is not conflicting — it is consistent membership evidence plus thin direct literature.

VERDICT: YES

**What the tools returned:**

1. **Identity & complex membership (UniProt).** Sm-D3 (SNRPD3, accession P62318, 126 aa) is a **core component of the spliceosomal Sm protein ring** — one of the seven common Sm proteins (SNRPB, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, **SNRPD3**, SNRPE, SNRPF, SNRPG) that assemble on the Sm site of snRNAs to form the core snRNP of the U1, U2, U4 and U5 snRNPs. 3. **Literature.** A focused search returned a directly on-topic clinical paper: **"Anti-Sm antibodies in the classification criteria of systemic lupus erythematosus" (van Beers & Schreurs, 2022)**, confirming that anti-Sm antibodies are part of the formal SLE classification criteria. Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35464346 (A related review on anti-ENA detection in systemic rheumatic disease: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/31887802.)

**Interpretation.** Per the autoantigen-status criteria I follow, a protein that UniProt documents as an **established core component of the Sm core/snRNP** — the particle detected by the named clinical **anti-Sm** antibody test — qualifies as an established SLE autoantigen on the strength of complex-level evidence plus documented core membership. UniProt confirms Sm-D3 is exactly such a core Sm component, and the literature confirms anti-Sm is an established, criteria-level SLE marker.

**Caveats for your review.** My literature queries did not surface a paper isolating anti-Sm-D3 *chain-specific* reactivity in SLE; the support for Sm-D3 specifically rests on its documented core-component status within the anti-Sm-reactive Sm particle, not on a D3-only clinical study. If you need chain-resolved serological data (e.g., SmD3 peptide ELISA performance), that would warrant a more targeted search.

VERDICT: YES

## Assessment: U1-70K (SNRNP70) as an SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity and complex membership**
- UniProt confirms SNRNP70 encodes "U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein 70 kDa" (accession P08621, 437 aa), and that it is one of the **U1 snRNP-specific proteins (SNRNP70/U1-70K)**, a core component of the U1 snRNP particle alongside SNRPA/U1-A and SNRPC/U1-C. (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P08621/entry)

Per the autoantigen-status criteria I follow, the U1 snRNP is a recognized SLE autoantigen complex captured by the named clinical **anti-U1-RNP** antibody test, and U1-70K is a documented core specific component of that particle. That membership alone is sufficient grounds to regard it as an established autoantigen.

**Literature evidence (reinforcing)**
- A 2015 study explicitly titled *"Mapping epitopes of U1-70K autoantibodies at single-amino acid resolution"* directly documents autoantibodies against U1-70K. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26333287)
- Utz et al. 2016 identified interferon-associated autoantibodies in SLE patients using multiplex biosensor arrays. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27279139)
- A 2006 murine model was induced using U1 snRNP autoantigen, confirming its immunogenic role. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/16453294)
- Additional master autoantigen-ome and autoantibody surveys list it among autoimmune-relevant targets. (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35237749; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33763057)

**Structural note (context only)**

**Caveat for the reviewer:** Anti-U1-RNP (and anti-U1-70K specifically) is a hallmark of mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) and is also well recognized in SLE; the clinical specificity is shared across these conditions. The tool evidence clearly establishes U1-70K as a recognized autoantigen within the U1-RNP system targeted in SLE.

VERDICT: YES

## Assessment: U1-A (SNRPA) as an SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity and complex membership.** UniProt confirms SNRPA encodes "U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein A" (accession P09012, 282 aa), and that it is one of the three U1 snRNP–specific proteins — SNRNP70/U1-70K, SNRPA/U1-A, and SNRPC/U1-C — alongside the seven Sm core proteins that form the U1 snRNP particle (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P09012/entry). This establishes U1-A as a recognized **core component of the U1 snRNP complex**, not merely an interactor.

**Why this matters for SLE classification.** Per the autoantigen criteria I follow, U1 snRNP is one of the recognized SLE autoantigen particles captured by a named clinical antibody test (anti-U1-RNP). A documented core component of that complex therefore qualifies as an established SLE autoantigen on the strength of complex-level evidence plus its documented membership — both of which UniProt provides above.

**Literature support.** Targeted searches returned published work on the U1-RNP autoantigen system in lupus and related connective tissue disease, including:
- "The Autoantigen Repertoire and the Microbial RNP World" (Williams & Wolin, 2021) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33722441
- "U1-RNP and TLR receptors in the pathogenesis of mixed connective tissue disease… The U1-RNP complex and its biological significance" (Paradowska-Gorycka, 2015) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27407234
- "Mapping epitopes of U1-70K autoantibodies at single-amino acid resolution" (Haddon et al., 2015) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26333287
- "Mixed Connective Tissue Disease and Epitope Spreading" (Escolà-Vergé et al., 2017) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/28248800
- "Mapping organ-associated autoantigenic landscapes in systemic lupus erythematosus" (Sosedskaia et al., 2026) — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42828094

**Caveat on the literature evidence.** My searches surfaced papers on the U1-RNP complex as a whole and specifically on the U1-70K chain, but I did not retrieve a paper in this session naming U1-A/SNRPA individually as the autoantibody target. The classification here rests on (1) UniProt's documentation of U1-A as a core U1 snRNP–specific component and (2) the published recognition of the U1-RNP complex as an SLE/MCTD autoantigen — which together satisfy the complex-membership criterion. An expert may wish to confirm chain-specific anti-U1-A reactivity if that granularity is needed.

**Structure note (context only, not disease evidence).** The AlphaFold predicted structure for P09012 has a mean pLDDT of 79.5 ("Confident") — https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P09012.

VERDICT: YES

These confirm that SLE autoimmunity targets nuclear/chromatin antigens, though none of the returned titles is a histone-H4-chain-specific paper.

UniProt documents Histone H4 as a core nucleosome component (not a mere interactor), which satisfies the complex-membership criterion. Complex-level evidence plus documented membership is sufficient; a chain-specific paper is not required.

My literature results were complex/disease-level reviews rather than an H4-specific primary study, so the paper-level support is general rather than chain-specific.
